title: Not knowing where I'm going
hook: his best-known prayer admits he doesn't know the road, but trusts the desire to please God pleases God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fourth and Walnut: a street corner where Merton saw strangers shining. Your line was they were shining. Did you catch the shine in anyone? Today, his most famous prayer. Day two hundred eighty-one.

Most of us are asked, sooner or later: so, what's the plan? After graduation. After the divorce. After the diagnosis, the layoff, the move. And most of us, if we're honest, don't have one. We fake it. We say something confident at the family dinner and lie awake afterward. Now imagine a famous monk, a man people wrote to for spiritual advice, putting on paper for everyone to read that he doesn't know where he's going. That's the opening of the prayer Thomas Merton is best known for. Today: not knowing where I'm going.
screen: `SO, WHAT'S THE PLAN?` → `WE FAKE IT.` → `HE DOESN'T KNOW WHERE HE'S GOING.`

segments.voice: First, where it's from. The prayer sits in a small book called Thoughts in Solitude, published in 1958. It's short, a single paragraph, and it's become one of the most shared prayers of the last century, printed on cards and read at graduations and funerals. Second, what it admits. Merton tells God, in his own words, that he doesn't see the road ahead or know where it ends. Then he goes further: he admits he doesn't really know himself, and that thinking he's following God's will doesn't mean he actually is. That's a startling thing for a monk to say. No false certainty at all. Third, the turn. Then comes the line people hold onto. Merton says he believes that the desire to please God does in fact please God. He hopes he has that desire in everything he does. And he trusts that if he keeps it, God will lead him by the right road, even when he can't tell. The desire counts, even when the map is missing. Fourth, the old roots. Scripture is full of people who set out without a map. The Letter to the Hebrews says of Abraham, in the Douay-Rheims: "he went out, not knowing whither he went." And the psalm says: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet." A lamp, not a floodlight. It lights the next step, not the whole road. Merton isn't praising confusion. He's saying faith can be honest. You're allowed to not know, as long as you keep wanting God.
screen: `THOUGHTS IN SOLITUDE, 1958.` · `I DON'T SEE THE ROAD AHEAD.` · `THE DESIRE TO PLEASE GOD PLEASES GOD.` · `A LAMP FOR THE NEXT STEP.` · then, large: `NOT KNOWING WHITHER HE WENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your not-knowing. Settle and breathe. Name one place in your life where you don't know the way. A decision. A relationship. A worry about what's next. Don't solve it. Just admit it, quietly: I don't know. Then notice whether, under the worry, there's a wanting, to do the right thing, to be good, to be close to God. If you pray, you can bring God both, the not-knowing and the wanting, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Not knowing where I'm going. The honest opening of Merton's best-known prayer, which trusts that wanting to please God already pleases God. Today's word.
screen: `NOT KNOWING WHERE I'M GOING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the desire counts. Today, when someone asks about the plan and you don't have one, try the truth: I'm not sure yet. Let the wanting be enough for one day. Day two hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray Merton's prayer from Thoughts in Solitude in times of discernment, and it's often printed on prayer cards and read at graduations, retreats and funerals.

fork.reveal: Merton admits he doesn't know, but trusts that the desire itself pleases God, and that God will lead him.

Merton's prayer from Thoughts in Solitude is under copyright and is described and paraphrased only, never quoted. Hook voice and screen were reworded to indirect speech ('he doesn't know where he's going') to stay clear of Merton's copyrighted opening line; the title/word 'Not knowing where I'm going' is kept as the outline gave it.
The practice invites the listener to bring the not-knowing to God in their own words; no new prayer is written.
